summary: Describes extended performance statistics for TCP, designed to use TCP's vantage point to diagnose problems in the network and in applications. It can help tell whether a slowdown comes from the sender, the receiver, or the network. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: TCP sits in the middle of every conversation and sees everything. This note lists the measurements it can report to find out who is slowing things down.

questions: what is the tcp extended statistics mib
how to diagnose tcp performance problems
how to diagnose a syn flood with snmp
how to tell if tcp or the network is the bottleneck
subtitle: A set of SNMP objects that let TCP report why a connection is slow: the sender, the receiver, the application or the network.

tldr.problem: When a network application performs poorly, it is hard to tell whether the bottleneck is the sender, the receiver, the application or the network path.
tldr.mechanism: The TCP-ESTATS-MIB exposes TCP's own estimators and state variables through SNMP, in seven tables and two groups of scalars, plus two notifications for new and closed connections.
tldr.outcome: Operators and implementers get a common way to read per-connection and per-listener statistics, with write access to the controls restricted for safety.

today: RFC 4898 is a Proposed Standard, published in May 2007. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends the TCP MIB of RFC 4022.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 4898 describes extended performance statistics for TCP. They are designed to use TCP's ideal vantage point to diagnose performance problems in both the network and the application. If a network-based application is performing poorly, TCP can determine whether the bottleneck is in the sender, the receiver or the network itself, and if it is the network, TCP can provide specific information about its nature.

The objects are Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP) objects that extend the TCP MIB of RFC 4022. In addition to several new scalars and other objects, the module augments two tables of RFC 4022 and makes one clarification to it. Existing management stations for the TCP MIB are expected to be fully compatible with that clarification. The module is named TCP-ESTATS-MIB and sits at { mib-2 156 }.
sections.eli5: TCP is like a referee who sees the whole game. This note gives the referee a scoreboard so we can tell whether the sender, the receiver or the road between them is the slow part.

sections.title: What the MIB Contains
sections.content:
The TCP-ESTATS-MIB consists of two groups of scalars, seven tables and two notifications.

  • The first scalar group has one object, tcpEStatsListenerTableLastChange, which helps management stations validate their listener caches.
  • The second scalar group holds the knobs that switch collection on and off, such as tcpEStatsControlPath for the path table, and tcpEStatsConnTableLatency, which sets how long connection rows are kept after a connection closes.
  • tcpEStatsListenerTable augments the listener table of RFC 4022 and supports diagnosing SYN-flood attacks.
  • tcpEStatsConnectIdTable augments tcpConnectionTable and maps a connection 4-tuple to an integer tcpEStatsConnectIndex, which indexes the five remaining tables and makes it quick to poll many objects of one connection.

The five per-connection tables split the work by question: performance, path behavior, stack behavior, application behavior and tuning controls. The two notifications are tcpEStatsEstablishNotification for a newly accepted or established connection and tcpEStatsCloseNotification for a connection that has recently closed.
sections.eli5: Think of a car dashboard with separate dials for the engine, the road and the driver. This MIB has separate tables for each part of a TCP conversation, plus switches to turn the dials on.

sections.title: Exposing Estimators, Not Prescribing Them
sections.content:
More than 70 RFCs and other documents specify aspects of TCP. TCP balances an application's need for fast, reliable transport against the need for fair use of the network, using many estimators and heuristics. RFC 2988, for example, describes how to compute the retransmission timer from the average and variance of the round-trip time. These algorithms are a compromise, optimal only for common Internet environments, and nearly all TCP documents leave latitude for improvement, so real implementations differ.

Because of that, the authors chose not to publish precisely defined network-path metrics that differ from what TCP uses. Instead the MIB exposes the estimators and important state variables that the implementation actually uses, possibly scaled or adjusted to match the object descriptions. The cost is that objects may not be exactly comparable between two TCP implementations. A general management station can assume only the abstract descriptions, while an implementer with detailed knowledge can use the MIB to debug or evaluate their own algorithms. The MIB is never intended to constrain TCP to use or exclude any particular estimator, heuristic, algorithm or implementation.
sections.eli5: Instead of making every player use the same stopwatch, the scoreboard just shows whatever each player's own stopwatch says. That means two scoreboards may not match exactly, but each tells the truth about its own player.

sections.title: Persistence and Row Retention
sections.content:
TCP is designed not to preserve state across reboots, so all objects in the MIB MUST have the same persistence properties as the TCP implementation. On a reboot, zero-based counters are cleared, dynamically created table rows are deleted and read-write objects return to their defaults. Implementations MAY choose to make the control scalars persist across reboots. The counters in the listener and connection tables start at zero when the row is created.

tcpEStatsConnTableLatency is the number of seconds an entity keeps entries in the connection tables after a connection first enters the closed state, so that final statistics can be read. Its default is 0, which removes entries as soon as the connection closes. When this MIB is implemented, it also gives meaning to the words "soon after" in RFC 4022's discussion of row deletion: all rows of all tables for one connection are kept at least that long after close. The control objects tcpEStatsControlPath, tcpEStatsControlStack, tcpEStatsControlApp, tcpEStatsControlTune and tcpEStatsControlNotify all default to false.
sections.eli5: When a conversation ends, the scoreboard can keep its numbers on the board for a set number of seconds so you have time to read them. After a restart, the board is wiped clean.

sections.title: Diagnosing SYN-Flood Attacks
sections.content:
The listener table is designed to help diagnose SYN-flood denial-of-service attacks, where a server is overwhelmed by forged or otherwise malicious connection attempts. Several defenses exist but none are standardized. They share two ideas: a well-defined moment when a connection is given full resources, and a backlog, a queue of embryonic connections that have only partial resources.

The RFC uses "accepting a connection" for the moment a connection is committed full resources, which in many implementations happens as a side effect of the POSIX accept() call. The backlog consists of connections in SYN-RCVD or ESTABLISHED state that have not yet been accepted. Some defenses, such as syn-cookies, dispense with an explicit SYN-RCVD state by encoding it in the initial sequence number of the SYN-ACK. The listener table therefore counts observable protocol events and resource-allocation events (entering the backlog, being accepted), which lets it work across defenses whose throttling algorithms differ too much to share one standard MIB.
sections.eli5: Imagine a restaurant that holds a waiting list before giving anyone a table. If fake callers fill the list, real guests are crowded out, so the host keeps counts of who called, who is waiting and who got seated.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Read-write and read-create objects may be sensitive. Changing tcpEStatsConnTableLatency or any control in the tcpEStatsControl group can affect the correctness of other management applications, so local policy should permit only limited write access, for example by one management station or only during system configuration. The tuning objects tcpEStatsTuneLimCwnd, tcpEStatsTuneLimSsthresh and tcpEStatsTuneLimRwin can limit resources used by connections or limit throughput, so an attacker might use them to degrade performance.

Readable objects can also be sensitive. Objects that expose TCP sequence numbers might make it easier for an attacker to forge in-sequence segments to disrupt connections, and nearly all objects may reveal traffic volumes. SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security. The RFC recommends SNMPv3 with its cryptographic authentication and privacy, and says deploying earlier SNMP versions is NOT RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: A scoreboard that anyone can change or read could be abused, so only trusted people should be allowed to flip its switches or look at its numbers.

items.title: Listener table
items.text: Extra information on active TCP listeners, including SYN-flood diagnosis.

items.title: Connection ID table
items.text: Maps a connection 4-tuple to the index used by the other tables.

items.title: Performance table
items.text: Objects for measuring TCP performance and first-check diagnosis.

items.title: Path table
items.text: Infers Internet path behavior such as segment loss or reordering.

items.title: Stack table
items.text: Shows how well TCP's control algorithms cope with the path.

items.title: Application table
items.text: Shows whether the application is limiting TCP performance.

items.title: Tuning table
items.text: Per-connection controls to work around common path problems.
